What Is a Model Card?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

In short: A model card is a short document that accompanies an AI model and reports what it is intended for, how it was evaluated, how it performs across different groups and conditions, what data it was trained on, and its known limits. The idea was proposed by Margaret Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 and is now the default format on model hubs. For a business buyer it is the first thing to read about a model, and the last word on nothing: it describes the model, not your use of it.

Key points

  • "Model Cards for Model Reporting" by Mitchell, Gebru and seven co-authors was presented at the FAT* conference in Atlanta in January 2019.
  • The paper proposed nine sections, from model details and intended use to quantitative analyses and ethical considerations.
  • Hugging Face's annotated template, used across its model hub, adds sections for out-of-scope use, environmental impact and how to get started.
  • The EU AI Act's Annex XII lists information general-purpose AI model providers must give downstream providers, including intended tasks, acceptable use policies, licence and training data.
  • CycloneDX, from version 1.5, can carry model card data inside a machine-readable AI bill of materials.

What a model card means

The original paper made a simple argument. Trained models were being released with no standard account of where they worked and where they failed. A short card, published with the model, would report performance broken down by the groups and conditions that matter, and say plainly which uses it was not meant for. The examples in the paper were a smiling-face detector and a toxic-comment classifier, but the authors said the format applies to any trained model.

The nine sections the paper proposed are still the core.

Section (Mitchell et al., 2019)What it records
Model detailsDeveloper, version, type, training approach, licence, contact
Intended usePrimary uses and users, and uses out of scope
FactorsGroups, instruments and conditions that may affect performance
MetricsPerformance measures, decision thresholds, how uncertainty is handled
Evaluation dataDatasets used for the reported results, and why
Training dataWhat the model learned from, at least its distribution across factors
Quantitative analysesResults by single factor and by combinations of factors
Ethical considerationsSensitive data, high-stakes uses, known harms and mitigations
Caveats and recommendationsRemaining concerns, gaps in evaluation, suggested further tests

How model cards are used now

Model hubs made the format routine. Hugging Face's annotated template splits intended use into direct, downstream and out-of-scope use, and gives a section to bias, risks and limitations, which it defines carefully: a bias is "a stereotype or disproportionate performance (skew) for some subpopulations", a limitation "a likely failure mode". It also asks for hardware, hours and estimated carbon emitted.

Regulation has picked up the same idea. Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII of the EU AI Act require providers of general-purpose AI models to give downstream providers information including the tasks the model is intended for, applicable acceptable use policies, release date, architecture and parameter count, input and output modalities, licence, and information on training, testing and validation data. That is a model card in all but name, and it is owed to firms that build products on the model.

Some model providers also publish longer "system cards" for their largest models, which usually add safety testing to performance. They are written by the developer too, and deserve the same reading.

How a buyer should read one

A 20 to 500 person firm rarely chooses a model directly. It chooses a tool that uses one. The model card still matters, because the tool inherits the model's limits.

Look forWhy it mattersWarning sign
Out-of-scope usesYour use may be listed as unsuitableYour use case appears on the list
Evaluation dataResults on unlike data say little about yoursOnly public benchmarks, none near your domain
Disaggregated resultsAverages hide weak groups or languagesOne headline number
Training data cut-off and sourcesAffects freshness and copyright exposureNo information at all
Version and dateCards describe one versionCard older than the model you are calling
LicenceGoverns commercial use, especially for open-weight modelsLicence differs from the vendor's claim

Two limits apply to every card. It is written by the developer, so it is a disclosure, not an audit. And it says nothing about your prompts, your data or your process. Testing that is your job; see What are AI evals?.

US banks have a separate documentation regime. SR 26-2, issued by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC on 17 April 2026, replaced SR 11-7 as model risk guidance; see What is model risk management? for its scope.

The lowob view

A model card describes the model. A firm also needs a record of each use: which tool, which model and version, what it is allowed to do, at what autonomy level, who approves its output and what outcome is expected. lowob keeps that as a line in the AI inventory, linked to the vendor's card. When the card changes because the model changed, the use line is where the firm decides whether its own approval still holds.

lowob takeaways

  • Read the out-of-scope section first. It is the quickest way to rule a model out.
  • Distrust single numbers. Useful cards report results by group and condition.
  • It is a disclosure, not an audit. The developer wrote it; test your own use.
  • Track the version. A card describes one model version, and vendors change models.

Common questions

What is a model card in machine learning?

A short document published with a trained model that reports its intended use, evaluation, performance across groups and conditions, training data and known limitations.

Who created model cards?

Margaret Mitchell and colleagues, in the paper "Model Cards for Model Reporting", presented at the FAT* conference in January 2019.

What is the difference between a model card and a system card?

A model card describes one model. System cards, published by some large providers, usually also cover the surrounding system and safety testing. Both are written by the developer.

Does the EU AI Act require model cards?

Not by that name. Annex XII requires general-purpose AI model providers to give downstream providers similar information, including intended tasks, licence and training data.

Sources and notes

  • Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting, arXiv:1810.03993, revised 14 January 2019. Peer-reviewed conference paper, FAT* 2019; the origin of the format.
  • Hugging Face, Annotated model card template, accessed November 2026. Platform documentation from a model hub vendor.
  • European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Annex XII, accessed November 2026. Primary legal text on information owed to downstream providers.
  • OWASP CycloneDX, Authoritative Guide to AI/ML-BOM, First Edition Revision 1, 10 June 2026. Open standard guidance; covers model cards inside an ML-BOM.
  • Federal Reserve, SR 26-2: Revised guidance on model risk management, 17 April 2026. Primary supervisory letter; applies to US banking organisations.

For your two most-used AI tools, ask the vendor which model and version each feature calls, and find that model's card. Note any out-of-scope use that matches yours on your AI inventory.
